sections.title: Reading Passage — Polyprotic Acids and Mixed Solutions
body: Polyprotic acids donate protons one at a time. For carbonic acid: H2CO3(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + HCO3−(aq) with Ka1 = 4.3 × 10−7, then HCO3−(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + CO32−(aq) with Ka2 = 4.7 × 10−11. Each step is harder because a proton must be pulled from a negatively charged ion, so Ka1 >> Ka2.
Because Ka1 dominates, [H3O+] for a diprotic acid is essentially set by the first ionization step alone. The second step contributes negligibly.

For mixed-solution problems, use the moles-first method: (1) convert every solute to moles, (2) react to completion — identify the limiting reactant and the leftover, (3) divide by the TOTAL volume, (4) calculate pH from the remaining strong acid, strong base, or weak conjugate pair.
The intermediate ion of a polyprotic acid (HCO3−, HSO4−, H2PO4−) is amphiprotic and buffers the solution between the two equivalence points of a titration.
common_mistakes: Writing both ionization steps in a single equation — polyprotic acids ionize one proton at a time.
Dividing by one solution's volume instead of the total volume after mixing.
Forgetting to check which reactant is the limiting reactant.

items.answer: One proton at a time (stepwise ionization)
items.explain: Each step has its own Ka; the first step dominates [H3O+].

items.q: For a diprotic acid, Ka1 is always ____ Ka2.
items.answer: Greater than (it is harder to remove a proton from a negative ion)
items.explain: Electrostatic attraction makes the second proton harder to remove.

items.q: In a 0.050 M solution of H2S, which species has the highest concentration?
items.answer: H2S (the acid itself — weak acids ionize only slightly)
items.explain: With Ka1 = 1.0 × 10−7, only ~0.1% ionizes, so H2S remains by far the most abundant species.

items.q: 50.0 mL of 0.100 M HCl mixes with 50.0 mL of 0.100 M NaOH. The resulting solution has pH:
items.answer: 7.00 (equal moles of strong acid and base exactly neutralize)
items.explain: Moles HCl = moles NaOH = 0.00500; complete neutralization leaves pure water with the salt.

items.q: 25.0 mL of 0.200 M HCl mixes with 75.0 mL of 0.050 M NaOH. The excess species is:
items.explain: Moles HCl = 0.00500, moles NaOH = 0.00375; leftover acid = 0.00125 mol in 0.100 L.

items.q: At pH 5.0, the dominant phosphate species is (pKa1 = 2.15, pKa2 = 7.20):
items.explain: Between the two pKa values, the singly deprotonated form dominates.

items.q: 30.0 mL of 0.100 M H2SO4 (diprotic, fully ionizing) provides how many moles of H+?
items.explain: Each H2SO4 molecule supplies two H+; multiply moles of acid by 2.

items.q: The intermediate ion HCO3− is best described as:
items.answer: Amphiprotic (can act as acid or base)
items.explain: HCO3− can donate a proton (→ CO32−) or accept one (→ H2CO3).

items.q: Calculate [H3O+] and pH for a 0.010 M solution of H2S (Ka1 = 1.0 × 10−7).
Calculate [H3O+] and pH for a 0.134 M solution of H2CO3 (Ka1 = 4.3 × 10−7).
50.0 mL of 0.100 M HCl is mixed with 50.0 mL of 0.060 M NaOH. Calculate the pH.
40.0 mL of 0.150 M KOH is mixed with 60.0 mL of 0.080 M HCl. Calculate the pH.
30.0 mL of 0.100 M H2SO4 is mixed with 70.0 mL of 0.050 M NaOH. Calculate the pH.
100.0 mL of 0.050 M HCN (Ka = 6.2 × 10−10) is mixed with 50.0 mL of 0.100 M NaOH. Calculate the pH.
Why does the second ionization of a diprotic acid contribute almost nothing to [H3O+]?
items.answer: Ka2 is typically 10^4–10^5 times smaller than Ka1 because removing a proton from a negatively charged ion is much harder; the tiny [HS−]-type intermediate ionizes barely at all, so its H3O+ contribution is negligible.

items.q: A student mixes 50 mL of 0.10 M HCl with 50 mL of 0.10 M NaOH and reports pH = 1. Explain the error.
items.answer: Equal moles of strong acid and strong base exactly neutralize: 0.0050 mol each, no leftover. The result is neutral salt water, pH = 7 — the student likely forgot to react the acid and base to completion.

items.q: Explain the moles-first method and why the total volume matters in mixed-solution calculations.
items.answer: Convert to moles, react to completion, then divide the leftover moles by the combined (total) volume to get concentration — pH depends on concentration, and the volume after mixing is the sum of both solutions.

items.q: For phosphoric acid (pKa1 = 2.15, pKa2 = 7.20, pKa3 = 12.35), which species dominates at pH 1.0, 5.0, 9.0, and 13.0?
